title: Missing CSRF Protection on Logout Endpoint
description: The logout endpoint at /logout uses HTTP GET method without any CSRF token validation. While the endpoint requires authentication (returns 401 without valid session), if a user is currently authenticated and visits a malicious website, that site could trigger logout via a simple GET request (e.g., or fetch() call), causing the user to be logged out without their knowledge or consent. The logout functionality does not require any CSRF token or additional confirmation mechanism to prevent cross-site request forgery attacks. The endpoint accepts GET requests (confirmed via OPTIONS method: Allow: OPTIONS, GET, HEAD) and does not enforce POST-only access patterns or implement SameSite cookie protections.
impact: An attacker can craft a malicious webpage that, when visited by an authenticated user, will automatically trigger logout without user interaction. While this primarily results in denial of service (session termination), it could be combined with other attacks such as phishing or credential harvesting. The logout uses GET method which is particularly vulnerable to CSRF attacks as GET requests can be triggered without JavaScript using simple HTML tags like ,
evidence: POC execution confirmed the following: 1. Logout endpoint accepts GET requests: curl -X GET http://localhost:5003/logout returns HTTP 401 (endpoint processes GET) 2. OPTIONS method shows allowed methods: Allow: OPTIONS, GET, HEAD - confirming GET is explicitly allowed 3. No CSRF tokens found in login page: grep for 'csrf' returns no results 4. POST method not allowed (HTTP 405) - only GET/HEAD/OPTIONS supported, making GET the only viable method for attackers 5. No SameSite cookie attributes detected on Set-Cookie headers 6. Attack vectors confirmed: - HTML image tag: - JavaScript fetch: fetch('http://localhost:5003/logout', {method: 'GET', credentials: 'include'}) - Automatic triggering on page load, no user interaction needed
remediation:
1. Implement CSRF token validation on the logout endpoint - require valid CSRF tokens in all logout requests
2. Change logout from GET to POST method, which is more resistant to CSRF as it requires explicit user action through XMLHttpRequest or form submission
3. Add SameSite cookie attribute set to 'Strict' on session cookie: Set-Cookie: session=...; SameSite=Strict; HttpOnly (prevents cookies from being sent to cross-site requests)
4. Consider requiring user confirmation before logout (e.g., password re-entry, security question, or additional click confirmation)
5. Implement CORS policy restrictions to prevent cross-origin requests to the logout endpoint
6. Use Flask-SeaSurf or similar CSRF protection middleware to automatically validate all state-changing requests
7. Add Referer/Origin header validation to ensure logout requests come from authorized origins
references: CWE-352: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), OWASP Top 10 2021 - A01:2021 Broken Access Control, RFC 7231 (HTTP/1.1 Semantics and Content) - GET should be idempotent
toolCallDescription: Document CSRF vulnerability on logout endpoint with confirmed POC
